# Supplement 2: Variance of the Cox model prediction
In the article, we assume the Cox model variance is estimated using the delta method. We use the derivation from the book \textit{Statistical Models Based on Counting Processes} by Andersen, Borgan, Gill and Keiding. Using this method, the variance of a Cox model prediction for the new patient is:

$$
V_{Cox}(\hat S_{new}(t)) = V(\hat S(t|x_{new})|\boldsymbol{\beta}) + \left. \frac{\partial S}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} \right|_{\boldsymbol{\beta}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^\top V(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) \left. \frac{\partial S}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} \right|_{\boldsymbol{\beta}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
$$

where $V(\hat{S}(t|x_{\text{new}})|\beta)$ is the variance of the survival function for a patient with covariates $x_{new}$, ignoring uncertainty in $\hat{\beta}$. The second term of the sum concerns the variance due to coefficient estimation and how this variance impacts the survival function by looking at the gradient of the survival function. The first term of the variance is given by:

$$
V(\hat{S}(t|\mathbf{x}_{\text{new}})|\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \hat{S}^2(t|\mathbf{x}_{\text{new}}) \exp(2\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top \mathbf{x}_{\text{new}}) \sum_{j:t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{\left(\sum_{i \in R_j} \exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)\right)^2}
$$

which is the Aalen formula for the variance of the baseline survival function based on the risk-weighted number at risk, multiplied by the risk score of our new patient.

The uncertainty in $\hat{S}_{\text{new}}(t)$ caused by the estimation of the coefficients depends on the variance of the coefficients and the gradient of the survival function with respect to the coefficients. The variance of the estimated coefficients $V(\hat{\beta})$ is asymptotically equal to the inverse Fisher information matrix $I(\hat{\beta})^{-1}$. Finally, we can estimate the gradient of the survival function with respect to the coefficient by:

$$
\left. \frac{\partial \hat{S}(t|x_{\text{new}})}{\partial \beta}\right|_{\boldsymbol{\beta}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = \exp(\beta^\top x_{\text{new}}) w
$$


where $w = (w_1, \dots, w_p)$ is a vector of partial derivatives, with $w_q$ the partial derivative of the survival function in the direction of $\beta_q$ for $q \in \{1, \dots, p\}$ with:

$$
w_q = \sum_{j:t_j \le t} \frac{1}{\sum_{i \in R_j} \exp(\hat\beta^\top x_i)} \left( \overline{x}_q - x_{\text{new},q} \right)
$$

where $\overline{x}_q$ is the risk-weighted mean of $x_{j,q}$'s ($\overline{x}_q=\frac{\sum_{i \in R_j} x_{i,q} \exp(\hat\beta^\top x_i)}{\sum_{i \in R_j} \exp(\hat\beta^\top x_i)}$), which are the $q$-th covariate for individuals $j$. Together, we have that the effective sample size for a Cox model prediction of a patient with covariate values $x_{\text{new}}$ at time $t$ is:

$$
N_*(t, x_{\text{new}}) = \frac{\hat{S}_{\text{new}}(t)(1-\hat{S}_{\text{new}}(t))}{\exp(2\hat\beta^\top x_{\text{new}}) \hat{S}_{\text{new}}^2(t) \left[ \sum_{j:t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{(\sum_{i \in R_j} \exp(\hat\beta^\top x_i))^2} + w^\top I(\hat{\beta})^{-1} w \right]}.
$$


# Supplement 3: Efficiency Breslow vs Nelson-Aalen

To understand why the effective sample size $N_*$ can exceed the development sample size $N$, we compare the variance of the hazard increments in a non-parametric setting versus the Cox proportional hazards setting.

In the absence of covariates, the Nelson-Aalen estimator for the cumulative hazard is $\hat{H}(t) = \sum_{t_j \leq t} \frac{d_j}{n_j}$. The variance of a single hazard increment at event time $t_j$ is given by:
$$
Var(\Delta \hat{H}_{NA}(t_j)) = \frac{d_j}{n_j^2}
$$
where $d_j$ is the number of events and $n_j$ is the number of individuals in the risk set $R_j$.

In the Cox model, the predicted hazard increment for a new patient with covariate profile $x_{new}$ is $\Delta \hat{H}_{new}(t_j) = \Delta \hat{H}_0(t_j) e^{\hat{\beta}^\top x_{new}}$. Considering only the variance component stemming from the baseline hazard (treating $\beta$ as fixed), the variance is:
$$
Var(\Delta \hat{H}_0(t_j) e^{\beta^\top x_{new}} \mid \beta) = (e^{\beta^\top x_{new}})^2 \frac{d_j}{(\sum_{i \in R_j} e^{\beta^\top x_i})^2}
$$

The Cox model provides a more precise estimate (lower variance) than the Nelson-Aalen estimator at time $t_j$ when:
$$
(e^{\beta^\top x_{new}})^2 \frac{d_j}{(\sum_{i \in R_j} e^{\beta^\top x_i})^2} < \frac{d_j}{n_j^2}
$$
Taking the square root and rearranging, this simplifies to:
$$
e^{\beta^\top x_{new}} < \frac{\sum_{i \in R_j} e^{\beta^\top x_i}}{n_j}
$$
This inequality demonstrates that the Cox model yields a lower prediction variance whenever the new patient’s risk score $e^{\beta^\top x_{new}}$ is lower than the arithmetic mean of the risk scores currently in the risk set $R_j$.

The informational efficiency of the Cox model stems from the proportional hazards assumption, which allows the model to utilize the entire longitudinal history of the cohort to estimate $\beta$. While the Nelson-Aalen estimator treats all individuals at risk as identical units, the Cox model utilizes their prognostic heterogeneity. For patients with a risk profile below the cohort average, this structural weighting reduces the stochastic noise of the baseline hazard estimation, leading to a variance lower than that of a standard binomial experiment and, consequently, an $N_* > N$.

# Supplement 4: Distribution of predictors
The first predictor was the `adhere` variable, a dichotomous indicator for adherence of the tumor to nearby organs (positive in 135 of 929 patients). The second predictor was `rx`, a three-level categorical variable of the three treatment arms from the randomized clinical trial. The third predictor was `age` as a continuous variable. The mean age was 60 years with a standard deviation of 12 years. The age distribution was left-skewed. Finally, the fourth predictor, `nodes`, was a heavily right-skewed variable (median 4 nodes, range of 0 to 33).

```{r}
#| label: supplement-4
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of 4 prognostic factors in the colon dataset."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| output: true
#| dev: png
#| dpi: 300


# Calculate the maximum frequency for bar plots
max_bar_freq <- max(table(colon_df$adhere), table(colon_df$rx))

# Calculate the maximum frequency for histograms
max_hist_freq <- max(table(cut(colon_df$age, breaks = seq(min(colon_df$age), max(colon_df$age) + 5, by = 5))),
                     table(colon_df$nodes))

# 1. Bar plot of frequency of adhere
plot1 <- ggplot(colon_df, aes(x = factor(adhere, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")))) +
  geom_bar(fill = col["b"], col = 'black') +
  labs(x = "Adherence", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylim(0, max_bar_freq)

# 2. Bar plot of frequency of rx
plot2 <- ggplot(colon_df, aes(x = factor(rx, levels = c("Obs", "Lev", "Lev+5FU"), labels = c("Obs", "Lev", "Lev+5FU")))) +
  geom_bar(fill = col["lp"], col = 'black') +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylim(0, max_bar_freq)

# 3. Histogram of age
plot3 <- ggplot(colon_df, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = col["r"], color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylim(0, max_hist_freq)

# 4. Histogram of nodes
plot4 <- ggplot(colon_df, aes(x = nodes)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = col["y"], color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Nodes", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal() +
  ylim(0, max_hist_freq)

library(patchwork)
combined_plot <- (plot1 | plot2) / (plot3 | plot4)
print(combined_plot)
```


# Supplement 5: Cox model has narrower 95% CI than Kaplan-Meier
The effective sample size of a prediction from a univariate Cox model based only on treatment is higher than that of a Kaplan-Meier curve for the same treatment group, especially early on in follow-up. This suggests that the Cox model prediction is more certain about the prediction and this should reflect in a smaller 95% confidence interval. Indeed, when comparing the Cox model prediction for a patient receiving 'Lev+5FU' treatment from univariate Cox model based only on treatment to the Kaplan-Meier curve for this treatment group in @fig-supplement-5, we see that the 95% confidence interval of the Cox model prediction is narrower than that of the Kaplan-Meier curve, especially early on in follow-up. This is consistent with the higher effective sample size of the Cox model prediction compared to the Kaplan-Meier curve for this patient and treatment group.

```{r}
#| label: fig-supplement-5
#| fig-cap: "95% Confidence Interval comparison."
#| output: true
#| echo: FALSE

source("code/compile.R")

colon_df$time <- colon_df$time/365.241

# Fit all the models
cox_adhere <- coxph( Surv(time, status) ~ adhere, data = colon_df)
cox_rx <- coxph( Surv(time, status) ~ rx, data = colon_df)

# Predict the effective sample size
km_adhere_0 <- survfit_n( survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = colon_df[colon_df$adhere == 0,]) )
km_adhere_1 <- survfit_n( survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = colon_df[colon_df$adhere == 1,]) )
km_rx_0 <- survfit_n( survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = colon_df[colon_df$rx == "Obs",]) )
km_rx_1 <- survfit_n( survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = colon_df[colon_df$rx == "Lev",]) )
km_rx_2 <- survfit_n( survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = colon_df[colon_df$rx == "Lev+5FU",]) )
cox_adhere_0 <- survfit_n( survfit(cox_adhere, newdata=data.frame(adhere=0)), cox=cox_adhere)
cox_adhere_1 <- survfit_n( survfit(cox_adhere, newdata=data.frame(adhere=1)), cox=cox_adhere)
cox_rx_0 <- survfit_n( survfit(cox_rx, newdata=data.frame(rx="Obs")), cox=cox_rx)
cox_rx_1 <- survfit_n( survfit(cox_rx, newdata=data.frame(rx="Lev")), cox=cox_rx)
cox_rx_2 <- survfit_n( survfit(cox_rx, newdata=data.frame(rx="Lev+5FU")), cox=cox_rx)


color_values <- c("Obs"= "#2E7691", "Kaplan-Meier" = "#C2666B", "Cox"= "#37293F", "Lev+5FU" = "#c6aa2c", "Adhesion" = "#9f84af")
linetype_values <- c("Prediction" = "solid", "95% CI" = "dashed")
plot_ci <- ggplot() +
  # Cox curves
  geom_line(aes(x = cox_rx_2$time, y = cox_rx_2$surv, color = "Cox", linetype = "Prediction"),
            lwd = 1.3, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(x = cox_rx_2$time, y = cox_rx_2$upper, color = "Cox", linetype = "95% CI"),
            lwd = 1.3, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(x = cox_rx_2$time, y = cox_rx_2$lower, color = "Cox", linetype = "95% CI"),
            lwd = 1.3, alpha = 0.5) +
  
  # Kaplan–Meier curves
  geom_line(aes(x = km_rx_2$time, y = km_rx_2$surv, color = "Kaplan-Meier", linetype = "Prediction"),
            lwd = 1.3, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(x = km_rx_2$time, y = km_rx_2$upper, color = "Kaplan-Meier", linetype = "95% CI"),
            lwd = 1.3, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(x = km_rx_2$time, y = km_rx_2$lower, color = "Kaplan-Meier", linetype = "95% CI"),
            lwd = 1.3, alpha = 0.5) +
  
  # Double arrow for Kaplan–Meier at t = 1.5
  geom_segment(
    {
      i <- which.max(ifelse(km_rx_2$time < 1.5, km_rx_2$time, -Inf))
      aes(x = km_rx_2$time[i], xend = km_rx_2$time[i],
          y = km_rx_2$lower[i], yend = km_rx_2$upper[i])
    },
    color = color_values["Kaplan-Meier"],
    linewidth = 1.2,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"), ends = "both", type = "closed")
  ) +
  
  # Double arrow for Cox at t = 1.6
  geom_segment(
    {
      j <- which.max(ifelse(cox_rx_2$time < 1.6, cox_rx_2$time, -Inf))
      aes(x = cox_rx_2$time[j], xend = cox_rx_2$time[j],
          y = cox_rx_2$lower[j], yend = cox_rx_2$upper[j])
    },
    color = color_values["Cox"],
    linewidth = 1.2,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"), ends = "both", type = "closed")
  ) +
  
  scale_color_manual(values = color_values) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = linetype_values) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Survival probability") +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Time (years)",
                     breaks = seq(0, max(colon_df$time), by = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Survival curve of a patient with Lev+5FU-treatment from Cox and Kaplan-Meier")
print(plot_ci)
```


# Supplement 6: Effective sample size of mean patient is $N$ in linear regression
To support a claim made in the article, we quickly show in an example with the GUSTO data that a patient with the mean value of all predictors in the model has an effective sample size equal to the development sample size in a linear regression model. We fit a linear regression model for the `day30` outcome based on age and height, two continuous predictors. We find that the effective sample size for a patient with mean age and mean height is 1214, equal to the development sample size of 1214 patients in this subset of the GUSTO data. We follow code from Thomassen 2024:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: supplement-6
#| output: true

library(Hmisc)
getHdata(gusto)
gusto.dat <- gusto[which(gusto$grpl %in% c(1,2,4) & gusto$grps %in% c(5,9,10,11)),]

gusto.dat$age <- gusto.dat$age - mean(gusto.dat$age)
gusto.dat$hei <- gusto.dat$hei - mean(gusto.dat$hei)

X_ols <- model.matrix(~age+hei, data=gusto.dat)
XTX <- t(X_ols)%*%X_ols

model <- lm(day30~age+hei, data=gusto.dat)
new <- matrix(c(1, 0, 0), nrow = 1, ncol=3)
A <- solve(XTX)%*%t(new)
n_eff <- 1/(new%*%A)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
print(paste0("Development sample size: ", nrow(gusto.dat)))
print(paste0("Effective sample size of a patient with mean height and age: ", n_eff))
```

# Supplement 7: Effective sample size for linear regression is bounded by number of patients in same category, but not for logistic regression

Effective sample size in linear regression models based on one continuous and one categorical variable are bounded by the number of patients in the same category. Below is an example in the GUSTO data for a linear regression model for height based on age and sex. There are 317 women in this subset of the data. First, we find that for a female patient with the population mean age, her effective sample size is 300, lower than the number of women in the data. However, if we calculate the effective sample size for a woman with the mean age of women, then the effective sample size is 317, equal to the total number of women in the data. 

```{r}
#| label: supplement-7
#| echo: FALSE
#| output: TRUE

model <- lm(height ~ age + sex, data = gusto.dat)
X_ols <- model.matrix(~age+sex, data=gusto.dat)
XTX <- t(X_ols)%*%X_ols
m_age <- mean(gusto.dat$age)
new <- matrix(c(1, m_age, 1), nrow = 1, ncol=3)
A <- solve(XTX)%*%t(new)
n_eff_1 <- 1/(new%*%A)

m_age_sex <- mean(gusto.dat[gusto.dat$sex == "female", "age"])
new <- matrix(c(1, m_age_sex, 1), nrow = 1, ncol=3)
A <- solve(XTX)%*%t(new)
n_eff_2 <- 1/(new%*%A)

print(paste0("Number of female patients: ", sum(gusto.dat$sex == "female")))
print(paste0("Effective sample size of a woman with population mean age from linear regression: ", round(n_eff_1)))
print(paste0("Effective sample size of a woman with female mean age from linear regression: ", round(n_eff_2)))
```

In logistic regression effective sample size can be higher then the total number of patients in your categorical subgroup, such as sex. To illustrate, we fit a logistic regression model for the `day30` outcome based on age and sex, again based on 1214 patients, 317 of which are women. Below is the same model based on age and gender, but now using a glm with logit link function. In a logistic regression model, the effective sample size can be higher than the amount of women in the data. The effective sample size for the prediction for a woman with the population mean age (406) is higher than that for a woman with the mean age among women (345). This contrasts with the linear regression model where effective sample size was the highest for the woman with the mean age among women. 

```{r}
#| label: supplement-7-2
#| echo: false
#| output: true

LR0.fit <- glm(formula = day30 ~ age + sex, data = gusto.dat, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
neff_1 <- c()
neff_2 <- c()

cov.beta <- vcov(LR0.fit)
X_LR0 <- model.matrix(LR0.fit)

new <- data.frame(age=mean(gusto.dat$age), sex="female")
pred <- predict(LR0.fit, newdata = new, type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
neff_1$pi.pred <- pred$fit
neff_1$pi.se <- pred$se.fit
neff_1$vary_xnew <- neff_1$pi.pred*(1-neff_1$pi.pred)
mm <- matrix(c(1, mean(gusto.dat$age), 1), nrow = 1, ncol = ncol(X_LR0))
neff_1$n_eff_LR <- 1/((mm %*% (cov.beta %*% t(mm)))*neff_1$vary_xnew)

new <- data.frame(age=mean(gusto.dat[gusto.dat$sex == "female", "age"]), sex="female")
pred <- predict(LR0.fit, newdata = new, type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
neff_2$pi.pred <- pred$fit
neff_2$pi.se <- pred$se.fit
neff_2$vary_xnew <- neff_2$pi.pred*(1-neff_2$pi.pred)
mm <- matrix(c(1, mean(gusto.dat[gusto.dat$sex == "female", "age"]), 1), nrow = 1, ncol = ncol(X_LR0))
neff_2$n_eff_LR <- 1/((mm %*% (cov.beta %*% t(mm)))*neff_2$vary_xnew)

print(paste0("Number of women in data: ", sum(gusto.dat$sex == "female")))
print(paste0("Effective sample size of a woman with population mean age from logistic regression without interaction: ", 
             round(max(neff_1$n_eff_LR))))
print(paste0("Effective sample size of a woman with female mean age from logistic regression without interaction: ", 
             round(max(neff_2$n_eff_LR))))
```


Next we include an interaction term between age and sex to the logistic regression model. Effective sample size is much lower for both predictions, with the effective sample size for a women with the population mean age dropping from 406 to 194 and for a women with the female mean age dropping from 345 to 235. Note that the effective sample size for a woman with the mean age in her subgroup of women, is now higher than for a woman with the mean age in the overall development population.

```{r}
#| label: supplement-7-3
#| echo: false
#| output: true

LR1.fit <- glm(formula = day30 ~ age + sex + age:sex, data = gusto.dat, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
neff_1 <- c(); m_age <- mean(gusto.dat$age)
neff_2 <- c(); m_age_women <- mean(gusto.dat[gusto.dat$sex == "female", "age"])

cov.beta <- vcov(LR1.fit)
X_LR1 <- model.matrix(LR1.fit)

new <- data.frame(age=m_age, sex="female")
pred <- predict(LR1.fit, newdata = new, type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
neff_1$pi.pred <- pred$fit
neff_1$pi.se <- pred$se.fit
neff_1$vary_xnew <- neff_1$pi.pred*(1-neff_1$pi.pred)
mm <- matrix(c(1, m_age, 1, m_age), nrow = 1, ncol = ncol(X_LR1))
neff_1$n_eff_LR <- 1/((mm %*% (cov.beta %*% t(mm)))*neff_1$vary_xnew)

new <- data.frame(age=m_age_women, sex="female")
pred <- predict(LR1.fit, newdata = new, type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
neff_2$pi.pred <- pred$fit
neff_2$pi.se <- pred$se.fit
neff_2$vary_xnew <- neff_2$pi.pred*(1-neff_2$pi.pred)
mm <- matrix(c(1, m_age_women, 1, m_age_women), nrow = 1, ncol = ncol(X_LR1))
neff_2$n_eff_LR <- 1/((mm %*% (cov.beta %*% t(mm)))*neff_2$vary_xnew)

print(paste0("Number of patients with your gender: ", sum(gusto.dat$sex == "female")))
print(paste0("Effective sample size of a woman with population mean age from logistic regression with interaction: ", 
             round(neff_1$n_eff_LR)))
print(paste0("Effective sample size of a woman with female mean age from logistic regression with interaction: ", 
             round(neff_2$n_eff_LR)))
```




# Supplement 8: Multivariable Cox effective sample size at 5 years with separate baseline hazards for treatment
Similar to figure 3 in the main text, but now with the model stratified by treatment instead of estimating a hazard ratio for treatment effect. At this 5-year survival prediction there is very little difference between the stratified and the non-stratified model, with the stratified model having slightly lower effective sample sizes, but not by much.
```{r}
#| echo: FALSE
#| output: TRUE
#| eval: FALSE
#| message: FALSE
#| warning: FALSE
#| fig-width: 10
#| label: supplement-8
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of effective sample size for the 5-year survival prediction in the data as a function of the predicted 5-year survival probability. The first model includes only treatment. The second model adds adhesion, the third model adds nodes and the fourth model adds age It can be seen that the effective sample size does not decrease for all patients with increasing variables, but it does for patients with rare covariate values."

#source("code/compile.R")

year <- 5
var1 <- "strata(rx)"; var2 <- "strata(rx) + adhere"; var3 <- "strata(rx) + adhere + nodes"; var4 <- "strata(rx) + adhere + nodes + age"
leg1 <- "Strata(Tx)"; leg2 <- "Strata(Tx) + Adh"; leg3 <- "Strata(Tx) + Adh + Nodes"; leg4 <- "Strata(Tx) + Adh + Nodes + Age"


# Single impute the nodes data
colon_df$nodes <- mice::complete(mice::mice(colon_df, m = 1, print = FALSE))$nodes

# Fit all cox models
cox_model1 <- coxph(as.formula(paste0( "Surv( time, status) ~ ", var1)), data = colon_df)
cox_model2 <- coxph(as.formula(paste0( "Surv( time, status) ~ ", var2)), data = colon_df)
cox_model3 <- coxph(as.formula(paste0( "Surv( time, status) ~ ", var3)), data = colon_df)
cox_model4 <- coxph(as.formula(paste0( "Surv( time, status) ~ ", var4)), data = colon_df)

# Create prediction df
out_df1 = out_df2 = out_df3 = out_df4 <- colon_df |>
  select( rx, age, adhere, nodes )
out_df1$model <- paste0( "(A) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var1)
out_df2$model <- paste0( "(B) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var2)
out_df3$model <- paste0( "(C) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var3)
out_df4$model <- paste0( "(D) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var4)


# Create SF object for correct time
sf1 <- summary( survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ rx, data = colon_df), time = year*365.25 )
sf1 <- data.frame(
  rx = factor(sub("^rx=", "", sf1$strata)),
  surv   = sf1$surv,
  std.err = sf1$std.err
) 
sf2 <- summary( survfit(cox_model2, newdata = out_df2), time = year*365.25 )
sf3 <- summary( survfit(cox_model3, newdata = out_df3), time = year*365.25 )
sf4 <- summary( survfit(cox_model4, newdata = out_df4), time = year*365.25 )

# Save survival probabilities
out_df1 <- merge(out_df1, sf1, by = "rx", all.x = TRUE)
out_df2$surv <- c(sf2$surv); out_df2$std.err <- c(sf2$std.err)
out_df3$surv <- c(sf3$surv); out_df3$std.err <- c(sf3$std.err)
out_df4$surv <- c(sf4$surv); out_df4$std.err <- c(sf4$std.err)

# Calculate the effective sample size for the 5-year prediction
out_df1$n.eff <- (1-out_df1$surv)*out_df1$surv/(c(out_df1$std.err)^2)
out_df2$n.eff <- (1-out_df2$surv)*out_df2$surv/(c(out_df2$std.err)^2)
out_df3$n.eff <- (1-out_df3$surv)*out_df3$surv/(c(out_df3$std.err)^2)
out_df4$n.eff <- (1-out_df4$surv)*out_df4$surv/(c(out_df4$std.err)^2)

out_df <- rbind(out_df1, out_df2, out_df3, out_df4)
out_df$model <- factor(out_df$model, levels = c(paste0( "(A) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var1), 
                                                paste0( "(B) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var2),  
                                                paste0( "(C) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var3), 
                                                paste0( "(D) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var4)))

# Create a scatter plot
colors <- c("#37293F", "#2E7691",  "#9f84af",  "#c6aa2c")
names(colors) <- c(paste0( "(A) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var1), 
                   paste0( "(B) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var2),  
                   paste0( "(C) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var3), 
                   paste0( "(D) Surv( time, status) ~ ", var4))

plot <- ggplot(out_df) +
  geom_point( aes(x = surv, y = n.eff, color = model), data = out_df, alpha = 0.2, size = 2) +
  facet_wrap( ~model ) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Predicted 5-Year Survival Probability", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Effective Sample Size", limits = c(0, 500)) +
  #ggtitle("Changes distribution of Eff. N. between models") +
  labs( color = "Legend") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = colors
  ) +
  #theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1)))

# Print the plot
plot
save(plot, file = "images/fig-distribution.RData" )
ggsave("4. Git Repository/images/distribution_strata.png", width = 13, height = 10, dpi = 300)
rm( list = ls())
```


# Supplement 9: Heuristic explanation of higher than total sample size
The baseline hazard for the Cox model at time $t_i$ with $\delta_i$ events is estimated as $\frac{d_j}{\sum_{i \in R_j} \exp( \hat\beta^\top \mathbf{x}_i ) }$, where the denominator is the risk-weighted number at risk. This risk-weighted number at risk is the implicit sample size used for the baseline hazard estimation and based on $\beta$, which is estimated based on all events including those in the future.

Near $t=0$ in Figure 4, a single death in 10,000 patients leads to a risk-weighted number at risk in the data of $5,000 \cdot 2 + 5,000 \cdot 1 = 15,000$. At such early follow-up time, the hazard of a patient is $\frac{\exp(\hat\beta^\top x_{\text{new}})}{\sum_{i \in R_j} \exp(\hat\beta^\top x_i)}$, the product of their hazard ratio and the baseline hazard. For a woman, the risk of being this first death is $1/15,000$, giving us an effective sample size of 15,000, exactly what was found in the simulation. For a man, the risk of being this first death is $2/15,000 = 1/7,500$, again matching the effective sample size of 7,500 in the simulation.

We can investigate this heuristic explanation in the simulation example as well:
```{r}
#| label: supplement-9
#| output: false
#| echo: false

require(surveillance)

# Seed for consistency
set.seed(1923)

scale = c(10)
shape = c(1) # shape 1 means exponential
maxtime = 100 # maxtime
hr = 2 # hazard ratio
n = 5000 # number per group

events <- simsurv( dist="weibull",
                   gammas=shape,
                   lambdas=scale[1]^(-shape),
                   x=data.frame(tx = c(rep(0, n), rep(1, n))),
                   betas = c("tx" = log(hr)),
                   maxt=maxtime)
events$tx = c(rep(0, n), rep(1, n))
events$eventtime[8885] <- 2.997671  # remove ties by hand
events$eventtime[6298] <- 5.668818  # because seed is set
time <- sort(unique(events$eventtime))
time0 <- sort(unique(events[events$tx == 0, ]$eventtime))
time1 <- sort(unique(events[events$tx == 1, ]$eventtime))

# Fit the models
sf0 <- survfit(Surv(eventtime, status) ~ 1, data = events[events$tx == 0,])
sf1 <- survfit(Surv(eventtime, status) ~ 1, data = events[events$tx == 1,])
cox <- coxph(Surv(eventtime, status) ~ tx, data = events)

# Calculate effective N and stuff
sf_n0 <- survfit_n(sf0) |> sf_to_df(time = time0)
sf_n1 <- survfit_n(sf1) |> sf_to_df(time = time1)
cox_n0 <- survfit_n(survfit(cox, newdata = data.frame(tx = 0)), cox, coef=T, chaz=T)
cox_n1 <- survfit_n(survfit(cox, newdata = data.frame(tx = 1)), cox, coef=T, chaz=T)

cox_n0 <- sf_to_df(cox_n0, time = time)
cox_n1 <- sf_to_df(cox_n1, time = time)
```

Our assumption/hypothesis is that the effective sample size at the beginning is this $\frac{HR_{new}}{Total risk}$ value. We cannot estimate variance before any events, so we analyse this hypothesis at the first event time. As we simulate with a HR of 2, we expect the total risk to be equal to $5000\cdot 1 + 5000 \cdot 2 = 15000$, the effective sample size for a female patient with HR of 1 should have an effective sample size of 15,000 (the denominator) and a male patient with HR of 2 should have an effective sample size of 7,500 (the denominator divided by HR).

The Cox model imperfectly estimates the hazard ratio, estimating it as: 1.98197. The expected effective sample size for women after one event, with this new assumed HR becomes 14910 (rounded to integer), and 7523 for men. However, we find that our effective sample size is estimated as 14907 for women and 7523 for men. The discrepancy for women may be caused by the variance from coefficient estimation, event if that is very small at this early time. If we assume the coefficient is perfectly estimated and only consider the variance caused by baseline hazard estimation, we find effective sample sizes of 14910 for women. This matches our hypothesis exactly. For men, it appears the impact of the coefficient estimation is too small to be a factor in the effective sample size at this early time.

```{r}
#| label: supplement-9-2
#| output: false
#| echo: false

print(paste0("The Cox model imperfectly estimates the hazard ratio, estimating it as: ", round(exp(cox$coefficients),5), ". The expected effective sample size for women after one event, with this new assumed HR becomes ", round(5000*exp(cox$coefficients)+5000) , " (rounded to integer), and ", round((5000*exp(cox$coefficients)+5000)/exp(cox$coefficients)), " for men. However, we find that our effective sample size is estimated as ", round(cox_n0$n.eff[1]), " for women and ", round(cox_n1$n.eff[1]), " for men. The discrepancy for women may be caused by the variance from coefficient estimation, event if that is very small at this early time. If we assume the coefficient is perfectly estimated and only consider the variance caused by baseline hazard estimation, we find effective sample sizes of ", round( (1 - cox_n0$surv[1])/ (cox_n0$surv[1] * cox_n0$std.chaz[1]^2)), " for women. This matches our hypothesis exactly. For men, it appears the impact of the coefficient estimation is too small to be a factor in the effective sample size at this early time."))
```



# Supplement 10: Heuristic explaination of asymmetry / variance attributable to coefficient
The asymmetry in predictions for equally exceptional patients based on a continuous variable can be explained in the same way. We find that the contribution of the coefficient uncertainty to the total variance for women drops off substantially from $t=7.5$ (Figure 4D). At the time of the first event $t_1$, the gradient (Equation 5, 6) for women ($\mathbf{x}_w$, equation 8) and men ($\mathbf{x}_m$, equation 9) is: 

$$\frac{\partial \hat{S}(t_1|\mathbf{x}_1=1)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} = \frac{\exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top \mathbf{x}_1)}{\sum_{i \in R_1} \exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)} \left\{ \frac{\sum_{i \in R_1} x_{i,q} \exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)}{\sum_{i \in R_1} \exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)} - x_{1,q} \right\} = \frac{1}{15000} \left\{ \frac{10000}{15000} - 0 \right\} = \frac{2}{450000} \quad (8)$$
$$\frac{\partial \hat{S}(t_1|\mathbf{x}_1=0)}{\partial \boldsymbol{\beta}} = \frac{\exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top \mathbf{x}_1)}{\sum_{i \in R_1} \exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)} \left\{ \frac{\sum_{i \in R_1} x_{i,q} \exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)}{\sum_{i \in R_1} \exp(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)} - x_{1,q} \right\} = \frac{2}{15000} \left\{ \frac{10000}{15000} - 1 \right\} = -\frac{2}{450000} \quad (9)$$
and because we multiply them (equation 3), sign cancels out. Therefore, the uncertainty from coefficient estimation is the same for both men and women since the variance of the coefficient is constant. Compare this to the gradient when there are twice as many women as men remaining in the risk set $(S_{women} (t_* )=2S_{men} (t_* ))$. At time $t_*$, the gradient changes $\left( \frac{\partial\hat S(t_*|\mathbf{x_{new}})}{\partial\mathbf{\beta}} - \frac{\partial\hat S(t_{*-1}|\mathbf{x_{new}})}{\partial\mathbf{\beta}}\right)$ by $\frac{1}{10000}$ for women and $\frac{-2}{10000}$ for men. With twice as many women alive as men, the distance from men to the population mean is now twice as high as for women and the gradient for men also changes at twice the rate as that for women. 

We need to investigate this at a time where we have quite a lot of knowledge of the ratio of the two groups in the data. At some point in time, the ratio between the two survival probabilities will be exactly 2. We will evaluate at this time $t$. We can find this by calculating:
$$ \frac{S(t| Woman )}{S(t | Man)} = 2 $$
$$ \log(S(t| Woman)) - \log(S(t | Man)) = \log(2) $$
$$ -H(t| Woman) + H(t| Man) = \log(2) $$
$$ -10t + HR\cdot 10 t = \log(2) $$
$$ t = \frac{10}{(HR - 1)}\log(2) $$

```{r}
#| output: true
#| echo: false

print(paste0("With our HR of ", round(exp(cox$coefficients), 5), ", this time becomes: ", round( (10/(exp(cox$coefficients) - 1))*log(2), 4), " time units."))
```

First, we look at the first event time and assume no one left the risk set. At the time of the first event, we assume that the number at risk in both groups is still $5000$. This means that $w_{men}$ is: $w_{men} = \frac{1}{5000+2\cdot 5000}\left\{\frac{2\cdot 5000}{5000+2\cdot 5000} - 1 \right\} = -\frac{1}{45000}$ and $w_{women} = \frac{2}{5000+2\cdot 5000}\left\{\frac{2\cdot 5000}{5000+2\cdot 5000} - 0 \right\} = \frac{2}{45000}$.

The gradient is $\mathrm{exp}(\beta^\top \mathbf{X}_{new})w$, which is $-\frac{2}{45000}$ for men and $\frac{2}{45000}$ for women. This is as expected, since men and women are both equally distant from the population mean in the risk set. Then the coefficient variance is (for one variable) the squared gradient times the variance of the coefficient, the last of which is constant.

At $t=6.913$, we can calculate the increment of the gradient by hand, which should be $2\cdot w_{men} = 2\cdot\frac{1}{2500+2\cdot 1250}\left\{\frac{2\cdot 1250}{2500+2\cdot 1250} - 1 \right\} = -2\cdot\frac{1}{10000}$ for men and $w_{women} = \frac{1}{2500+2\cdot 1250}\left\{\frac{2\cdot 1250}{2500+2\cdot 1250} - 0 \right\} = \frac{1}{10000}$ for women. We see that the increment of the gradient is now twice as high for men.


# Supplement 11: Logistic regression has higher variance than Cox regression
We can show that the variance of a logistic regression prediction is higher than that of a Cox regression prediction for the same patient in a simulation with no censoring. We simulate data on 10,000 patients with a time-to-event outcome based on a single continuous predictor $X\sim N(0,1)$ with a hazard ratio of 2 and an exponential baseline hazard with scale 10. We fit a Cox and make survival predictions at time $t$ and fit a logistic regression model on the outcome at time $t$ and predict at time $t$. We make these predictions with the Cox at time $t=0.01$ and $t=2$ and fit logistic regression models on the observed outcomes at these times.

```{r}
#| label: supplement-11
#| echo: false
#| output: false

set.seed(1923)

X <- rnorm(10000, 0, 1)
hazard_ratio <- 2
shape <- 1 # shape 1 means exponential
scale <- 10 # scale parameter for the Weibull distribution

df <- simsurv( dist="weibull",
               gammas=shape,
               lambdas=scale[1]^(-shape),
               x=data.frame(X = X),
               betas = c("X" = log(hazard_ratio)),
               maxt=100)
df$X <- X

# Evaluate outcome at t=5 and generate log.reg event
df$status_start <- ifelse(df$eventtime <= 0.01, df$status, 0)
df$status_at_t <- ifelse(df$eventtime <= 2, df$status, 0)
df$time_1 <- ifelse(df$eventtime >= 0.01, df$eventtime, 0.01)
df$time_2 <- ifelse(df$eventtime >= 2, df$eventtime, 2)

glm1 <- glm(status_start ~ X, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = df)
glm2 <- glm(status_at_t ~ X, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = df)
cox <- coxph( Surv(eventtime, status)~X, data = df)
cox_1 <- coxph( Surv(time_1, status_start)~X, data = df)
cox_2 <- coxph( Surv(time_2, status_at_t)~X, data = df)

mean <- as.data.frame(t(c(X=0)))

## ---- glm1 ----
pred1 <- predict(glm1, newdata = mean, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)

eta1  <- -pred1$fit
se1   <- pred1$se.fit

# 95% CI on link scale
lwr1  <- eta1 - 1.96 * se1
upr1  <- eta1 + 1.96 * se1

# Transform to probability scale
fit1 <- list()
fit1$pi.pred <- plogis(eta1)
fit1$lower   <- plogis(lwr1)
fit1$upper   <- plogis(upr1)
fit1$pi.se_link <- se1

# optional: delta-method SE on probability scale
fit1$pi.se_resp <- fit1$pi.pred * (1 - fit1$pi.pred) * se1
fit1$n_eff_LR <- (fit1$pi.pred*(1-fit1$pi.pred)) / fit1$pi.se_resp^2


## ---- glm2 ----
pred2 <- predict(glm2, newdata = mean, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)

eta2  <- -pred2$fit
se2   <- pred2$se.fit

lwr2  <- eta2 - 1.96 * se2
upr2  <- eta2 + 1.96 * se2

fit2 <- list()
fit2$pi.pred <- plogis(eta2)
fit2$lower   <- plogis(lwr2)
fit2$upper   <- plogis(upr2)
fit2$pi.se_link <- se2
fit2$pi.se_resp <- fit2$pi.pred * (1 - fit2$pi.pred) * se2
fit2$n_eff_LR <- (fit2$pi.pred*(1-fit2$pi.pred)) / fit2$pi.se_resp^2


sf <- survfit(cox, newdata = mean, model = T)
sf <- survfit_n(sf, cox) |> sf_to_df(time = c(0.01, 2))
sf_1 <- survfit(cox_1, newdata = mean, model = T)
sf_1 <- survfit_n(sf_1, cox_1) |> sf_to_df(time = 0.01)
sf_2 <- survfit(cox_2, newdata = mean, model = T)
sf_2 <- survfit_n(sf_2, cox_2) |> sf_to_df(time = 2)

sf$surv[1]/(fit1$pi.pred)
sf$surv[2]/(fit2$pi.pred)
sf_1$surv/(fit1$pi.pred)
sf_2$surv/(fit2$pi.pred)

(sf$surv[1]^2*sf$std.err[1]^2)/fit1$pi.se_resp^2
(sf$surv[2]^2*sf$std.err[2]^2)/fit2$pi.se_resp^2
(sf_1$surv^2*sf_1$std.err^2)/fit1$pi.se_resp^2
(sf_2$surv^2*sf_2$std.err^2)/fit2$pi.se_resp^2

sf$n.eff
fit1$n_eff_LR
fit2$n_eff_LR
sf_1$n.eff
sf_2$n.eff

(sf$upper[1]-sf$lower[1])/(fit1$upper-fit1$lower)
(sf$upper[2]-sf$lower[2])/(fit2$upper-fit2$lower)
(sf_1$upper-sf_1$lower)/(fit1$upper-fit1$lower)
(sf_2$upper-sf_2$lower)/(fit2$upper-fit2$lower)

```

The prediction at $t=0.01$ for both models is nearly identical (0.00003% difference), with any difference being explained by finite sample behaviour, rather than bias. The variance of the Cox model prediction is only 66% of the logistic regression model variance. This also results in a much larger effective sample size for the Cox model prediction compared to the LR: 12684 vs 8722. The width of the confidence interval from the Cox model is only 75.7% that of the logistic regression model. When comparing it to the Cox model fit on the data restricted to $t=0.01$, we see that the variance of the Cox model prediction is only over 99% of the logistic regression model variance, showing that most of the increased efficiency of the Cox model comes from the estimation of the coefficients based on data throughout the follow-up. Effective sample size is also the same for the restricted Cox model compared to logistic regression.

At $t=2$ the predictions are again nearly identical (0.006% difference). The variance of the Cox model prediction is much lower, at 79% of the logistic regression variance. This is also reflected in the effective sample size, as the Cox model still has higher effective sample size at 10561 compared to 8489 for the LR model. The width of the confidence interval from the Cox model is only 88.7% that of the logistic regression model. When restricting the Cox model to data up to $t=2$, we see that the variance of the Cox model prediction is 97% of the logistic regression model variance. The effective sample size of the Cox model prediction has now similarly increased to 200 above the logistic regression model estimate. This indicates the increased efficiency over a logistic regression model due to knowing the survival times in addition to the status at time $t=2$.


# Supplement 12: Average hazard ratio in the data is above 1
The explanations in section 4 are based on simulations where all hazard ratios are above 1, resulting in a risk-weighted number at risk that is higher than the development sample size. One could suggest changing the reference category and reduce the risk-weighted number at risk. If men were the reference category and women the alternative with a hazard ratio of $0.5$, then the risk-weighted number at risk would be 7,500. The risk for men would be  1/7,500 and the risk for women $\frac{0.5}{7500}=\frac{1}{15000}$, providing the same heuristic effective sample size as before.

After normalizing variables by centering and rescaling, the mean hazard ratio in the development data will be above 1. For a $N(0,1)$ variable with a HR of 2, the mean linear predictor in the data is 0, but the mean HR is not equal to 1, since $\mathbb{E}[\text{exp}(X\beta)]\not = \text{exp}(\mathbb{E}[X\beta]))$. As an example, for $X \sim N(0,1)$ and a HR of 2, $\mathbb{E}[\text{exp}(X\ \text{ln}2)] = \text{exp}(\frac{\text{ln}2^2}{2})\approx 1.2715$. This transformation increases the risk-weighted number at risk to naturally be larger than the development population, which contributes to the larger effective sample sizes of Cox model predictions for patients with the population mean risk.

We can investigate this in practice:
```{r}
X = rnorm(1000000, 0, 1)
HR = 2
beta = log(HR)

lin_pred = beta*X
HRs = exp(lin_pred)

mean(lin_pred)
mean(HRs)
```

So we observe that the mean linear predictor (X\beta) is 0 (ignoring some monte-carlo standard error), while the mean hazard ratio is 1.27. 

```{r}
N = 1000000
p = 0.5
X = c(rep(0, N*(1-p)), rep(1, N*p))
HR = 2
beta = log(HR)

X = X - p
X = X/sqrt(p*(1-p))

lin_pred = beta*X
HRs = exp(lin_pred)

mean(lin_pred)
mean(HRs)
```
Similarly, we can consider a case where we have one categorical covariate with two categories. This is usually presented as a 0-1 scenario with a beta that only counts for the 1 category. This can be represented by a +1/-1 scenario with a beta that is half as high as well. In this situation, the mean linear predictor in the population is again 0, but the mean hazard ratio is again above 1.

A more complicated example can be illustrated in the colon data, if we rescale all variables first.

```{r}
colon_df_scaled <- colon_df
colon_df_scaled$age <- c(scale(colon_df_scaled$age))
colon_df_scaled$nodes <- c(scale(colon_df_scaled$nodes))
colon_df_scaled$adhere <- c(scale(colon_df_scaled$adhere))
# add dummy variables for rx and rescale
colon_df_scaled$rx1 <- ifelse(colon_df_scaled$rx == "Obs", 1, 0)
colon_df_scaled$rx2 <- ifelse(colon_df_scaled$rx == "Lev", 1, 0)
colon_df_scaled$rx3 <- ifelse(colon_df_scaled$rx == "Lev+5FU", 1, 0)
colon_df_scaled$rx1 <- c(scale(colon_df_scaled$rx1))
colon_df_scaled$rx2 <- c(scale(colon_df_scaled$rx2))
colon_df_scaled$rx3 <- c(scale(colon_df_scaled$rx3))

cox <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + nodes + adhere + rx1 + rx2 + rx3, data = colon_df_scaled)
mean(cox$linear.predictors)
mean(exp(cox$linear.predictors))

neff <- survfit_n(survfit(cox, newdata = data.frame(age=0, nodes=0, adhere=0, rx1=0, rx2=0, rx3=0)), cox) |> sf_to_df(time = colon_df_scaled$time)
```

Again in such an example we see that the mean linear predictor in the Cox model based on age, nodes, adhere and treatment is 0 (with some small finite-sample error), while the mean hazard ratio in the population is 1.10. For a patient with the mean covariate values, this would already imply that their effective sample size would be above the total sample size of 911 patients. And indeed, the effective sample size for a patient with a 0 for all covariate values is 1008 at the first event time, which is close to the expected 911*1.1046 = 1006. The small difference can be explained by differences in population means due to the 18 patients with missing values in any of the variables.


# Supplement 13: Cox model predictions confidence intervals have good coverage
We suggest a Cox model based on two variables, one binary and one continuous and investigate the coverage for a few patients with different covariate values. Our variables are $X_1$ binary assigned with a Bernoulli($0.5$) distribution and $X_2$ continuous assigned with a $N(0,1)$ distribution. We assume a HR of 2 for both variables and a constant baseline hazard of 1. Each iteration is with $N=1000$. To estimate the coverage, we use $1999$ replications. 

We see that coverage is good at 95% across all time points just after the start, even though effective sample size is higher than the development sample size throughout. Only at the very beginning is there under coverage, but this is because the first event has not taken place in all of the simulation runs and before the first event there is always under coverage.
```{r}
source("code/sim_files.R")
sim_coverage( reps = 1999, newpatient = data.frame(X1=0, X2=0))
sim_coverage( reps = 1999, newpatient = data.frame(X1=1, X2=0))
sim_coverage( reps = 1999, newpatient = data.frame(X1=0, X2=-1))
```


# Supplement 14: Model-based standard errors are equal to Monte Carlo standard errors
Additionally, we check the model-based standard errors against the empirical standard errors for the same simulation as in the previous section (Supplement 11). We find that they are extremely close, which indicates that the model-based standard errors are accurate and that the effective sample size calculations based on these standard errors are also accurate. There are indications of a slight overestimation of the standard error early on in follow-up, which could be responsible for any slight overcoverage early on in follow-up.
```{r}
sim_se_comparison( reps = 5000, newpatient = data.frame(X1=0, X2=0))

sim_se_comparison( reps = 5000, newpatient = data.frame(X1=1, X2=1))
```

# Supplement 15: Effective sample size in open real-world datasets

To investigate how often the behaviour described in the main text occurs in practice, we computed effective sample sizes for Cox models fitted to eight open datasets (colon, pbc, veteran, lung, rotterdam, gbsg, flchain, mgus2; optionally support). For each dataset we pre-specified a set of candidate predictors (skewed positive biomarkers were log-transformed beforehand) and fitted a Cox model (Efron ties) with backward elimination on AIC. The delta-method variance does not account for the selection step, so $N_*$ is conditional on the selected model. For every patient in the development data, $N_*$ was calculated at the time points at which 1%, 10%, 25%, 40%, 60%, 75% and 90% of all events had occurred. Because N* is expressed relative to the development sample size, results are reported as $N_*/N$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-supplement-15-setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("code", "ess_realworld.R"))
cache <- here::here("results", "ess_realworld.rds")
if (file.exists(cache)) {
  res <- readRDS(cache)
} else {
  res <- run_all()
  dir.create(dirname(cache), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  saveRDS(res, cache)
}
sm <- summarise_ess(res)
pl <- make_plots(res, here::here("results"))
```

# Supplement 16: Simulation studies of the behavior of $N_*$ (ADEMP)

Two simulation studies are reported in Section 4. Simulation 1 describes $N_*$ early in follow-up, without censoring, in a single binary or continuous predictor. Simulation 2 describes $N_*$ over the whole follow-up in a model with multiple predictors, for a wide range of overall event rates, model strengths and censoring patterns. Both are reported according to the ADEMP framework (aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, performance measures) [@morris2019].

## Simulation 1: early follow-up and the first-event heuristic

**Aims.** (1) To show that $N_* > N$ occurs early in follow-up for patients with a lower hazard than the average patient. (2) To show how the variance of the survival estimate is divided into a part from the baseline hazard and a part from the coefficient, and how this division changes over time. (3) To compare $N_*$ at the first events with the heuristic $N_* \approx N \cdot \overline{\mathrm{HR}} / \mathrm{HR}_i$.

**Data-generating mechanisms.** $N = 10\,000$ patients without censoring, constant baseline hazard $h_0(t) = 1$ and one predictor with hazard ratio 2: either a binary $X_1$ (exactly half of the patients with $X_1 = 1$) or a continuous $X_2 \sim N(0,1)$.

**Estimands.** The survival probability and its effective sample size for patients with $X_1 = 0$ and $X_1 = 1$, and for patients with $X_2 = -1, 0$ and $1$, over time.

**Methods.** A Cox model with the predictor was fitted to the data and $N_*$ was calculated with Equations (2) and (3). The variance was split into the baseline hazard term and the coefficient term. For the binary predictor, Kaplan-Meier estimates in the two groups were used as a reference.

**Performance measures.** $N_*$ over time, and the proportion of the variance that originates from the baseline hazard.

**The first-event heuristic.** At the first event time $t_1$, $\widehat{H}_0(t_1) = 1 / \sum_{j} \mathrm{HR}_j$ and its variance is $1 / (\sum_{j} \mathrm{HR}_j)^2$. For a patient with hazard ratio $\mathrm{HR}_i$, $\widehat{S}_i \approx 1 - \mathrm{HR}_i / \sum_j \mathrm{HR}_j$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{S}_i) \approx \mathrm{HR}_i^2 / (\sum_j \mathrm{HR}_j)^2$, so that
$$N_* = \frac{S(1-S)}{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{S})} \approx \frac{\sum_j \mathrm{HR}_j}{\mathrm{HR}_i} = N \cdot \frac{\overline{\mathrm{HR}}}{\mathrm{HR}_i},$$
with $\overline{\mathrm{HR}}$ the mean hazard ratio in the development data. For the binary predictor, $\overline{\mathrm{HR}} = 1.5$, so $N_* \approx 15\,000$ for $X_1 = 0$ and $7\,500$ for $X_1 = 1$. The coefficient term is negligible at the first event and grows with the number of events.

## Simulation 2: when does $N_*$ exceed $N$, and is $N_*$ reliable?

### Aims

1. To determine for which true survival probabilities the estimated effective sample size exceeds the development sample size ($\widehat{N}_* > N$), and how this depends on the overall proportion of patients with an event, the strength of the model (Harrell's C of the true linear predictor) and the type of censoring.
2. To determine whether the variance underlying $\widehat{N}_*$ is reliable, which is assessed by the coverage of the 95% confidence interval. $N_*$ is the prediction variance re-expressed with the binomial variance, so a large $N_*$ is only meaningful if the variance is accurate.

### Data-generating mechanisms

Event times followed a Weibull proportional hazards model with $H_0(t) = t^{\gamma}$ and $\gamma = 1$. The model contained three standard normal and three binary (prevalence 0.5) true predictors with equal contributions to the linear predictor (coefficients 1 and 2, respectively). All coefficients were multiplied by a constant such that Harrell's C of the true linear predictor equalled a target value. This was determined in a large sample, truncated at the time at which the target proportion of patients had experienced an event.

The main simulation was a full factorial design with three factors (40 scenarios):

- Harrell's C of the true linear predictor: 0.6, 0.7, 0.8 and 0.9.
- Overall proportion of patients with an event, $e$: 5%, 10%, 30%, 60% and 90%. The sample size was $N = 500 / e$ so that every scenario contains about 500 events ($N = 10\,000$ for $e = 5\%$ and $N = 556$ for $e = 90\%$).
- Censoring: either a common end of follow-up for all patients, or administrative censoring mimicking registry data with staggered inclusion. In the latter, the potential follow-up of each patient was uniformly distributed between 20% and 100% of the maximum follow-up (for example, between 1 and 5 years), so nobody was censored early. The maximum follow-up was calibrated such that the overall proportion of patients with an event was $e$.

Sensitivity analyses varied one factor at a time (Section "Sensitivity analyses"): the number of predictors ($k = 1, 3, 10$ continuous and $k$ binary predictors), the addition of $k$ predictors unrelated to the outcome, the Weibull shape ($\gamma = 0.7, 1, 1.5$) and random censoring (loss to follow-up).

### Estimands

The estimand is the true survival probability $S(t \mid x)$ for 200 fixed covariate profiles, located at quantiles 0.0005, 0.002, 0.01 to 0.99, 0.998 and 0.9995 of the true linear predictor, at seven time points. These are the times at which 5%, 10%, 25%, 40%, 60%, 75% and 90% of all events in the population had been observed. The reference effective sample size is
$$N_*^{\text{true}} = \frac{S(1-S)}{\operatorname{Var}_{\text{emp}}(\widehat{S})},$$
with $\operatorname{Var}_{\text{emp}}$ the variance of $\widehat{S}(t \mid x)$ over the replications.

### Methods

In each replication a Cox model (Efron ties) with all predictors (true predictors and, where applicable, noise predictors) was fitted. $\widehat{S}$ and its delta-method standard error were obtained with `survfit`, and $\widehat{N}_* = \widehat{S}(1-\widehat{S})/\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat{S})^2$. Confidence intervals were calculated on the log-log scale.

### Performance measures

For each prediction (covariate profile, time point, simulated dataset) the true survival probability $S$ is known from the data-generating model, and $\widehat{N}_*$ is calculated from the fitted model. The primary measure is the percentage of predictions with $\widehat{N}_* > N$ among all predictions with the same true $S$; equivalently, the probability that a prediction for a patient with true survival $S$ has $\widehat{N}_* > N$. Predictions are grouped by $S$ on the logit scale (bins of 0.2 to 0.4). The other measures, calculated per scenario, profile and time point, are the ratio of the mean estimated variance to the empirical variance, and the coverage of the 95% confidence interval. All measures are shown as a function of the true survival probability on the logit scale (symmetric around 0.5), pooled over the time points, Harrell's C values and censoring settings, with every prediction weighted equally; the supplementary figures show them separately. The profiles are equally spaced quantiles of the linear predictor, so each stands for the same share of the population, and the percentage over all predictions at a time point is the share of the population with $\widehat{N}_* > N$. Profiles at the extremes of the linear predictor (below the 1st and above the 99th percentile) are extrapolations in a sample of this size and are excluded from the summaries. The true survival at which the percentage of predictions with $\widehat{N}_* > N$ crosses 5% was determined (by interpolation) for each event rate, and for each scenario separately for the table. Its relation with the overall event proportion $e$ was described by $1 - S^* = a\,e^{b}$, fitted by least squares on the log-log scale.

### Number of replications

The number of replications was determined in a pilot ($R = 300$ in selected scenarios, including the most demanding ones): the Monte Carlo standard error of each performance measure was estimated per cell (time point by band of true survival), and the number of replications was chosen such that the 90th percentile of the required numbers met a Monte Carlo standard error of 1 percentage point for $P(\widehat{N}_* > N)$, 0.5 percentage points for coverage and 5% for the variance ratio. This gave $R = $ <!-- fill in from pilot_mc() --> replications per scenario.

### Limitations

The fitted model is correctly specified, apart from the noise predictors in the sensitivity analysis, and no variable selection is performed. The simulation therefore isolates the behavior of the variance estimator. Misspecification, variable selection and overoptimism are not investigated. Predictions with a true survival below 0.01 rely on very few events in the replications, and their empirical variances are imprecise.

## Sensitivity analyses

These analyses were run for the reference scenario ($C = 0.7$ unless stated otherwise) and varied one factor at a time. Estimands, methods and performance measures were as in Simulation 2.

**Number of predictors and noise predictors.** $k = 1, 3, 10$ continuous and $k$ binary true predictors, with and without $k$ added predictors unrelated to the outcome ($N = 1000$, 90% of patients with an event, common end of follow-up; design `oat`).

**Weibull shape.** The reference scenario with only the shape changed ($\gamma = 0.7, 1, 1.5$; design `shape_only`). The Cox model is invariant to monotone transformations of time, so the estimates, and hence $N_*$, are identical up to the calibration of the scale. The shape can only matter when the censoring distribution is tied to the time scale, as in the next analysis.

**Random censoring.** Administrative censoring off or on, combined with random censoring (loss to follow-up, independent exponential) of intensity 0 (none), 1 (regular; 10% of patients lost by the maximum follow-up if no event occurs first) or 5 (severe; five times the hazard of loss), at overall event rates of 10%, 30% and 60% and $C = 0.7$ (design `censoring`).

# Supplement 17: Effective sample size from a bootstrapped variance

The effective sample size $N_*$ in the main text uses the delta-method variance of the Cox model survival estimate (Equation 2 of the main text). Any other variance estimator can be used in its place. Here we compare the delta-method variance with the bootstrap variance for the colon cancer data, using both a non-parametric and a parametric bootstrap, to check that the effective sample size does not depend on the variance estimator.

## Methods

We used the colon cancer data of the main text (overall survival, 929 patients; number of positive nodes imputed once, as for Figure 3) and the four sequential Cox models of Section 3.3: (A) treatment; (B) treatment and adherence; (C) treatment, adherence and nodes; (D) treatment, adherence, nodes and age. For each model, survival was predicted for every patient in the development data at 1 to 7 years. The delta-method variance of $\widehat{S}(t \mid x)$ was taken from `survfit()` as in the main text.

For the bootstrap variance, $B = 1000$ bootstrap samples were generated in one of two ways. In the non-parametric bootstrap the 929 patients were drawn with replacement. In the parametric bootstrap [@thomassen2025] the covariates of the 929 patients were kept and new outcomes were simulated from the Cox model fitted to the original data: event times were drawn from the fitted model with the Breslow estimate of the baseline hazard, and censoring times from the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the censoring distribution, independently of the covariates. In each bootstrap sample the same Cox model was refitted (Efron ties), the cumulative baseline hazard was estimated, and the survival probability was predicted for the *original* patients' covariate values. The bootstrap variance of $\widehat{S}(t \mid x)$ is the variance of these predictions over the bootstrap samples. For both variances the effective sample size is

$$N_* = \frac{\widehat{S}(1 - \widehat{S})}{V(\widehat{S})},$$

with $\widehat{S}$ the estimate from the original fit, so that the two estimates differ only in the variance. We compare them per patient and horizon by the ratio $N_*^{\text{boot}} / N_*^{\text{delta}}$ (summarised in the table). The Monte Carlo error of a variance estimated from $B = 1000$ samples is about $\sqrt{2/(B-1)} = 4.5\%$ (relative), so ratios within about $\pm 10\%$ of 1 are indistinguishable from this error. Neither bootstrap repeats the imputation of the number of nodes, so, like the delta-method variance, both are conditional on the model specification and the imputed data. The parametric bootstrap additionally assumes that the fitted Cox model and an independent censoring distribution describe the data.

```{r}
#| label: sim-supplement-17-run
#| include: false
source(here::here("code", "compile.R"))
source(here::here("code", "bootstrap_ess.R"))
cacheB <- here::here("results", "ess_bootstrap_colon.rds")
if (file.exists(cacheB)) {
  resB <- readRDS(cacheB)
} else {
  resB <- run_colon_bootstrap(years = 1:7, B = 1000)
  dir.create(dirname(cacheB), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  saveRDS(resB, cacheB)
}
smB <- summarise_boot(resB)
```

## Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-supplement-17-scatter-np
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Effective sample size from the non-parametric bootstrap variance against effective sample size from the delta-method variance for all 929 patients, at 5 years, for the four models of Figure 3 (log-log scale). Dashed line: equality."
plot_boot_scatter(resB, year = 5, type = "nonparametric")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-supplement-17-scatter-p
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "As Figure S17.1, with the variance from the parametric bootstrap."
plot_boot_scatter(resB, year = 5, type = "parametric")
```

The two bootstraps and the delta-method variance give similar effective sample sizes (Figures S17.1 and S17.2). For models A and B, which contain only the binary treatment and adherence variables, the patients form a few groups and the estimates coincide. For models C and D, the bootstrap estimates follow the line of equality over most of the range, with the non-parametric bootstrap tending to give somewhat lower values than the delta-method variance for patients with a low effective sample size, i.e. patients with less common covariate values. The parametric bootstrap lies closer to the delta-method estimate. A few patients with a high delta-method $N_*$ have a much lower bootstrap $N_*$ in models C and D, in both bootstraps.
